newsitem.title: UK: New UK budget assumptions don't justify tax rises.
newsitem.headline: New UK budget assumptions don't justify tax rises.

text.p: New economic assumptions made by the British government for economic growth and public borrowing on Thursday are modest and provide no ready-made excuse for big tax rises in the July 2 budget, analysts said.

"There are no big black holes in the UK public finances, according to the National Audit Office," said David Walton, UK economist at Goldman Sachs. "It is not obvious why (Chancellor of Exchequer) Gordon Brown would feel any need to raise taxes on the back of this report."

The Treasury lowered medium-term economic growth forecasts, and calculated that had these new assumptions been in place at the time of the last budget, corresponding PSBR forecasts would have been higher.
But economists were quick to point out the adjustments to PSBR forecasts were small and, in the short-term especially, would be swamped by the dramatic improvement in the PSBR.

"The implications for the PSBR are pitifully small. The Treasury did not change the growth forecast for this year and the chances are it will be even higher than forecast, driving the PSBR down even further," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan.

Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch agreed. "The report was certainly not as apocolyptic as some talk suggested. The changes made to the baseline assumptions for the PSBR will be swamped by cyclical effects."
He noted the PSBR is on a steady downtrend, even better than predicted in the November budget, thanks to improved tax take and impressive spending restriant.

The Treasury said using its new assumptions, the 1997/98 PSBR would be 500 million stg higher than the 19.2 billion foreacst in November, and 3.25 billion higher than the 12 billion pounds forecast for 1998/99.

Revisions to the later years were more dramatic, but the budget finances are still set to head into the black in fiscal year 2000-01 according to the new assumptions, just a year after the previous government's forecast.
The assumptions add 4.0 billion stg to the 1999-2000 projection of 3.0 billion stg, and 7.0 billion stg to the 8.0 billion stg surplus forecast for 2001/02.
"But given the errors in forcasting that far ahead, it makes little difference," said Mackie.
Brown is set to deliver his first budget on July 2, and speculation has grown that he is casting round for excuses to raise taxes.
There are still economic arguments for tightening fiscal policy, but the current state of the public finances is not one of them, analysts said.

"There are still reasons for raising taxes, namely that fiscal policy should play a part in demand management, and the structural deficit maybe too high, but the idea of a black hole in the public finances is ludicrous," said Mackie.

Given the strength of UK economic growth, if Brown does not tighten fiscal policy in July the newly empowered Bank of England is likely to push up interest rates very sharply. Those economist who foreacst such an outcome see rates hitting 7.5 percent compared with 6.50 percent currently.
